title: Office Suite Market Share: Microsoft, Google, LibreOffice — CIO Monitor

Office Suite Market Share: Microsoft, Google, LibreOffice — CIO Monitor

November 8, 2026

# One Point of Office Suite Market Share Is Now Worth $1 Billion a Year

Office productivity software hit $50.73B in 2025 and may reach $81.83B by 2030. Per Vignoli, cheap OOXML clones save money but hand Microsoft control of the content.

By Tom Whitfield November 8, 2026 3 min read

Cam feed · SIG-4239 APP

Feed Office Suites: Cheaper Isn’t Necessarily Freer — Dan Counsell / unsplash

## Event log

1. T+01 Office productivity software market: $50.73B in 2025, forecast $81.83B by 2030 (10.1% CAGR).
2. T+02 Microsoft 365 Commercial generated $102B in FY2026, up 16%; Copilot paid licenses exceeded 30 million by end of June 2026.
3. T+03 6sense: 64% of organizations use both Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace.
4. T+04 Estimated 1% of market share is worth about $1 billion a year to a commercial vendor.
5. T+05 LibreOffice downloads +26% and donations +44% as of October 31, 2026.

One percentage point of office suite market share is worth roughly $1 billion a year to a commercial vendor. That single figure, derived from Business Research Company forecasts, explains why low-cost clones and AI-built suites keep arriving — and why, according to The Document Foundation co-founder Italo Vignoli, most of them change nothing about who actually controls your documents.

The office productivity software market reached $50.73 billion in 2025, per the "Office Productivity Software Market Report 2026" by Business Research Company. It is expected to hit $81.83 billion by 2030, a 10.1% CAGR. Add value-added consultancy — which Vignoli estimates at about 25% of license value — and the 2030 total approaches $102 billion.

## What do the giants actually earn?

The headline numbers sit with the incumbents. Microsoft 365 Commercial generated $102 billion in fiscal year 2026, up 16%. Paid Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses passed 30 million by the end of June 2026, which analysts put at 6–7% of the paid commercial base.

Google Workspace counts over 3 billion users and more than 11 million paying customers, though the user figure includes free Gmail accounts and is not comparable to Microsoft's paid subscriptions. 6sense technographic data attributes 50.34% of the office productivity category to Google Workspace and 45.46% to Microsoft 365, based on corporate domains. Measured in corporate licenses and revenue, Microsoft leads clearly.

## Who runs both suites?

According to 6sense, 64% of organizations use both suites. For LibreOffice, Vignoli estimates from hands-on work with large organizations that 50% of its users also run another suite, depending on their needs. Overlap, not exclusivity, is the norm.

## What does this change for buyers?

The core argument is blunt. OOXML is formally an ISO standard, but its reference implementation remains with Microsoft. As long as that holds, Vignoli writes, "Microsoft retains control over the content: the user saves money, but sacrifices digital sovereignty." He defines sovereignty as the ability to open documents with any implementation, fork the code, and choose where data is hosted and who operates the service.

The history explains the current position. Microsoft Office took over 90% market share — per Microsoft's own unofficial statements at its events — by the end of the 1990s, outlasting Lotus SmartSuite, WordPerfect Office and StarOffice. Sun Microsystems released the StarOffice source in 2000; OpenOffice.org 1.0 followed in 2002, and only version 2.0 in 2005 became a genuine competitor.

Since 2012, Microsoft has ranked among the biggest spenders on lobbying in Brussels, according to Corporate Europe Observatory and Lobby Facts data. The format battle ran from ODF's ISO/IEC standardization in 2006 to OOXML's in 2008. In 2010, after Oracle acquired Sun, the community founded The Document Foundation and LibreOffice. In 2011, Oracle effectively had to donate the OpenOffice.org code to Apache to honor an IBM contract, due to expire in 2014. IBM then abandoned its ODF advocacy at OASIS to fund Apache OpenOffice and fight LibreOffice's growth.

The sovereignty question resurfaced in 2024 with large migrations: the German province of Schleswig-Holstein and the Austrian Army both announced moves to open source.

## Are clones and AI suites a real threat?

Vignoli is skeptical. New clones compete on license cost, support OOXML natively, and some release "source-available" basic versions that fail the Open Source Definition — proprietary freeware, in practice, with a full-featured edition sold separately. They target cheap replacement, not migration. On AI-developed suites, he says he remains "extremely cautious" and is monitoring closely.

The strategic point stands regardless: if reproducing a feature set becomes cheap, features stop being the barrier. What remains is format governance, code governance, community strength and long-term maintenance.

LibreOffice itself is growing. As of October 31, 2026, downloads were up 26% and donations up 44%. Vignoli's verdict: LibreOffice and ODF compete on a different axis — open governance of format and code, not feature parity at a lower price. With around 2 billion desktop and laptop devices in the installed base, the market has room for everyone. Whether buyers choose control or a discount is the decision that actually matters.
